name: Beirut
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Beirut: asset tracing after the banking collapse, port-related claims and Beirut-seated arbitration support.
hero_lede: Investigative consulting for matters touching Beirut, scoped from Nashville: asset tracing and counterparty research after Lebanon's financial collapse, factual support for counsel in Beirut-seated arbitrations and court proceedings, and diligence on businesses and property affected by the 2020 port explosion and later conflict.
intro: Beirut is Lebanon's capital and the centre of its banking, trade, media and professional services. For decades the city served as a regional financial hub, with Lebanese banks, the central bank Banque du Liban and many family trading groups headquartered there. Its port is the country's main gateway, handling 61 percent of Lebanon's merchandise imports and 41.2 percent of its exports in the first five months of 2025. The city has absorbed successive shocks: the financial collapse that began in 2019, the explosion of 4 August 2020, which killed more than 200 people and caused damage the World Bank estimated at 4.6 billion dollars, and the impact of later conflict. Businesses have rebuilt largely with private and diaspora funds.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Beirut because the financial crisis left creditors, depositors and investors with unresolved claims and limited visibility over where assets went. Lenders and counterparties need to know which Beirut groups remain solvent, which have moved assets abroad, and who controls companies whose shareholders sit behind nominees or offshore vehicles. Insurers, contractors and claimants still deal with disputes from the port explosion. Beirut-seated arbitrations, including claims against financial institutions over losses linked to the collapse, need well-sourced facts on parties and assets. Exposure to designated persons and entities makes sanctions screening essential in almost every Beirut matter.

matters.title: Asset tracing after banking collapse
matters.text: Research for creditors, depositors' counsel and investors seeking to understand where Beirut-based individuals, groups or financial institutions moved assets after 2019, drawing on registries, property records, court filings and foreign corporate records to identify holdings outside Lebanon that may be relevant to recovery.

matters.title: Family group and nominee structures
matters.text: Mapping ownership of Beirut trading, real estate and services groups whose shareholders appear through nominees, holding companies or offshore vehicles, using commercial register extracts, beneficial ownership disclosures where available and foreign registries, so clients know who controls a counterparty.

matters.title: Beirut-seated arbitration support
matters.text: Assembling factual material for counsel in arbitrations administered by LAMC or seated in Beirut, including banking-crisis claims, commercial disputes and enforcement, covering the opposing party's corporate structure, related companies, assets and prior litigation before the Beirut courts.

matters.title: Port explosion claims research
matters.text: Supporting insurers, contractors and claimants in disputes arising from the August 2020 port explosion, by researching the businesses, property owners and intermediaries involved, their insurance and corporate histories, and how ownership of affected properties has changed since the blast.

matters.title: Sanctions and integrity screening
matters.text: Screening Beirut counterparties, shareholders and intermediaries against sanctions lists and adverse media, with attention to links to designated persons or entities, politically exposed persons and banking-sector figures, before any contracts, investments, payments or settlements are allowed to proceed.

local_context.title: Beirut courts
local_context.text: Commercial disputes involving Beirut companies are typically heard by the first-instance courts in Beirut, with appeal to the Beirut Court of Appeal and final review by the Court of Cassation, which also sits in the city. The Beirut Court of First Instance grants exequatur to arbitral awards, as it did in late 2024 in a banking-crisis arbitration. Courts have faced strikes and resource constraints, so timelines and record availability can be unpredictable.

local_context.title: LAMC and Beirut arbitration
local_context.text: The Lebanese Arbitration and Mediation Centre of the Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture of Beirut and Mount Lebanon was established in 1995 and revised its rules comprehensively in 2024, adding consolidation, joinder, expedited procedures and emergency arbitrators. The Beirut Bar Association's centre, LIAC-BBA, presented updated rules in 2025, and the first Beirut Arbitration Days took place that May. Banking-crisis disputes are increasingly arbitrated in Beirut.

local_context.title: Chamber and commercial register
local_context.text: The Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture of Beirut and Mount Lebanon is the city's main business body and host of LAMC. Company records for Beirut entities are held by the commercial register attached to the Beirut court of first instance, where extracts show shareholders, board members, signatories and recorded lawsuits or seizures. Land registry certificates are a separate and often more revealing source on property holdings.

local_context.title: Port of Beirut after 2020
local_context.text: The explosion of 4 August 2020 was caused by nearly 3,000 tonnes of improperly stored ammonium nitrate. The World Bank estimated about 350 million dollars in damage to the port, whose most heavily damaged section had still not been rebuilt by mid-2025, although the container terminal operates normally. The domestic investigation has been repeatedly stalled and no senior official had been convicted as of August 2025.

tdsc_approach: For matters touching Beirut, TDSC first screens the matter for sanctions exposure and declines any engagement that would involve designated persons or entities in breach of US or other applicable sanctions. TDSC then defines the question, whether that is tracing assets, identifying who controls a group or preparing facts for an arbitration, and maps which Beirut and foreign records can answer it. Research is conducted from Nashville using register extracts, property certificates obtained through counsel, published decisions and Arabic, French and English sources. Where in-country retrieval or interviews are needed, TDSC coordinates with qualified local professionals and Lebanese counsel, mindful of banking secrecy and communications laws.

faqs.q: Can you trace assets moved out of Beirut after the 2019 financial crisis?
faqs.a: We can research lawfully available records in Lebanon and abroad, including corporate registries, property records, court filings and press, to identify holdings connected to a person or group. We cannot access bank account information protected by Lebanese banking secrecy. Where formal disclosure is needed, we work with counsel to identify the court or arbitral procedures that can obtain it.

faqs.q: How useful is a Beirut commercial register extract?
faqs.a: It is often a strong starting point, showing legal form, capital, shareholders, board members, authorised signatories and recorded lawsuits or seizures. Extracts may be outdated or show nominees, and capital figures in Lebanese lira have lost meaning since the currency collapse, so we corroborate them with property records, foreign registries and other sources.

faqs.q: Can you support a LAMC arbitration or a Beirut exequatur application?
faqs.a: Yes, by supplying factual research to counsel on the opposing party, its related companies, assets in Lebanon and abroad, and prior disputes. Applications to the Beirut courts are made by Lebanese counsel. Because enforcement can be delayed by annulment proceedings, we often also look for assets in other jurisdictions where an award might be enforced.

faqs.q: Why does almost every Beirut matter need sanctions screening?
faqs.a: Designations by the US and other governments have covered Lebanese individuals, companies and financial institutions, and ownership links are not always visible. We screen counterparties, shareholders and intermediaries before accepting a matter and as research proceeds, and we decline engagements that would conflict with US or other applicable sanctions.

faqs.q: Does TDSC have an office in Beirut?
faqs.a: No. TDSC is based in Nashville and has no office or staff in Beirut or elsewhere in Lebanon. Most of our work is desk-based research. Where on-the-ground steps are required, we coordinate with qualified local professionals working lawfully and alongside the client's Lebanese counsel, and we avoid methods that would breach secrecy or privacy laws.
